A Google Ads responsive search ad is not one ad you write; it is a pool of up to 15 headlines and 4 descriptions that Google assembles into combinations and shows according to the search. For a Pune business paying for clicks, the practical answer to "how do I write a good one?" is: write headlines that each stand alone, cover different angles instead of repeating one, pin only what legal or brand rules require, include the location and the offer where they are true, and then judge the ad by leads and cost per lead, not by the Ad Strength label. This guide is for owners and marketers who run, or pay a digital marketing agency in Pune to run, Google Ads Search campaigns and want to understand what is actually happening inside the ad.

It covers how responsive search ads work, how to plan the headline pool, character limits and writing rules, when pinning helps and when it hurts, how to read asset reports honestly, what to do about Ad Strength, and a simple testing routine for accounts with modest budgets.

## How responsive search ads work

When you create a responsive search ad (RSA), you supply headlines and descriptions. Google's current help documentation says you can enter up to 15 headlines of up to 30 characters each and up to 4 descriptions of up to 90 characters each, and the system tests combinations to learn which perform best for different searches ([Google Ads Help: About responsive search ads](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7684791)). An ad displays up to three headlines and up to two descriptions at a time, depending on the format, and the order and combination can vary from one impression to the next.

Three consequences follow, and they shape everything below:

1. **Every headline must make sense next to any other headline.** You do not control which three appear together, so a headline that only works as "headline one" is a liability.
2. **You are writing a pool, not a script.** Coverage matters more than polish: offer, proof, location, service, action.
3. **You cannot A/B test one sentence in the old way.** RSAs rotate combinations automatically, so you learn from asset-level reports and from the ad's overall results, with caveats covered below.

If you are new to how clicks are priced and ranked, read our explanation of [Quality Score, Ad Rank and cost per click](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-quality-score-ad-rank-cost-per-click-2026) first; ad relevance and expected click-through rate are two of the inputs, and your headlines affect both.

## Start from the search, not from the ad

The best ad copy starts with a list of what people actually type. Before writing, gather:

- **Your search terms report**, to see real phrasings, including Hinglish or Marathi-English mixes and neighbourhood names. Our guide to the [search terms report and negative keywords](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-negative-keywords-search-terms-report-2026) shows how to read it.
- **Your ad groups' keyword themes.** Each ad group should cover one tight theme, such as "2BHK interior design Pune" or "physiotherapy for back pain Kothrud". Write the ad for that theme, not for the whole business.
- **Customer questions**: what do people ask on the phone before they buy? Price? Timeline? Whether you visit their home? Those questions are your angles.
- **What the landing page says.** The ad promises; the page delivers. If an ad says "Free site visit" and the page never mentions it, expect wasted clicks and a poor experience. Our note on [landing pages versus the homepage for ads](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-landing-page-vs-homepage-ads-2026) covers matching ad and page.

## A headline pool that covers different angles

Fifteen headlines of the same idea reworded do little. A better method is to assign slots by angle. A workable plan for a local service business:

| Angle | Slots | Example pattern (illustrative) |
|---|---|---|
| Service and keyword | 3 to 4 | "Interior Designer in Pune" |
| Location | 1 to 2 | "Serving Baner, Aundh and Wakad" |
| Offer or action | 2 to 3 | "Book a Free Site Visit" |
| Proof | 2 to 3 | "Verified Google Reviews" |
| Process or differentiator | 2 to 3 | "One Team, Design to Handover" |
| Price or risk reversal | 1 to 2 | "Written Quote Before You Pay" |

The examples above are patterns, not claims about any real firm. Use only statements you can honour. If you do not offer a free site visit, do not write it. The same applies to numbers: "500+ projects", "since 2009" and "4.8 rating" must be true on the day the ad runs and must be checkable.

### Headline writing rules that hold up

- **Fit the 30-character limit with whole words**, not clipped phrases. Test how each reads alone.
- **Put the searcher's own words in at least a few headlines.** If people search "AC repair in Pune", say "AC Repair in Pune" in at least one headline rather than only "Cooling Solutions".
- **Vary the openings**, so combinations do not read like "Pune Interior Designer | Interior Designer Pune | Best Interior Designer".
- **Use sentence or title case consistently**, and avoid all-caps and gimmicky symbols. Google's editorial policies restrict excessive capitalisation, repeated punctuation and gimmicky formatting; check the current rules before using them.
- **Do not make claims you cannot prove.** "Best", "No. 1" and "guaranteed" need substantiation and can lead to disapproval or customer complaints. If you advertise a price, it must match what the customer will see.
- **Avoid trademarks you do not own** in ad text unless policy allows it; see Google's trademark policy before naming a competitor or brand in an ad.
- **Include a call to action in at least a couple of headlines**: "Call Today", "Get a Quote", "Book Online". Make sure the landing page offers the same action.

## Descriptions: four chances to answer the next question

You have up to four descriptions, each up to 90 characters. A headline gets the click; a description answers the objection that would otherwise stop it. Use them for:

1. **What you do and for whom, in one sentence.**
2. **How it works or what is included**, such as "Design, carpentry and finishing handled by one team."
3. **Proof or reassurance**: reviews, registrations, years in business (only if true).
4. **The next step and any condition**: "Call or WhatsApp for a written quote. Mon-Sat, 10am-7pm."

Each description should be self-contained, ending with a full stop or a clear stop, since any pair may be shown together. Do not repeat the same sentence across descriptions.

## Location and phone details belong in assets, not only in text

Several text details are better handled with ad assets (formerly extensions), which sit alongside your ad:

- **Sitelinks** to your pricing page, services pages and contact form.
- **Callouts** for short points such as "Free site visit" or "Weekend appointments".
- **Structured snippets** for lists such as service types.
- **Call assets** with your tracked phone number, tied to your business hours. See our guide to [call tracking for Google Ads phone leads](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-call-tracking-phone-leads-2026) for setup and the privacy points to cover.
- **Location assets** linked to your Business Profile, which can help local searchers see your address and distance.
- **Image assets** where Google offers them for your campaign type.

Assets do not replace good headlines, but they widen your ad's footprint and answer more questions before the click. Check that each asset's wording follows the same honesty rule as your headlines.

## Pinning: use sparingly and know the cost

Pinning lets you fix a headline or description to a specific position (for example, always show a particular headline in position 1). The same Google Ads documentation notes that pinning reduces the number of possible combinations and can reduce the ad's flexibility and performance.

Good reasons to pin:

- **A legal or regulatory statement** that must always appear, such as a mandatory disclaimer in a regulated category. (Take advice from a qualified professional on what your sector requires.)
- **Brand name in position 1** when brand consistency is truly required.
- **A required offer condition**, such as a minimum order or an eligibility note, which would mislead if omitted.

Weak reasons to pin:

- "We just like that headline best."
- Pinning three different headlines to positions 1, 2 and 3 so the ad is effectively a fixed old-style expanded text ad. That removes most of the reason for using an RSA.

If you pin, **pin more than one headline to the same position** (for example, two or three alternatives for position 1) so the system still has choices. Review the effect on impressions and conversions after a few weeks rather than assuming pinning helped.

## Ad Strength: a guide, not a goal

Google shows an Ad Strength rating (from Poor to Excellent) as feedback on how well your ad follows its guidance on variety and relevance. It can be useful as a checklist: it may prompt you to add more distinct headlines, include keywords or avoid repetition.

But it is not a measure of business results. An ad rated "Excellent" can bring unqualified clicks, and a "Good" ad can bring the best leads. Treat Ad Strength as follows:

- **Use it to find obvious gaps**, such as too few headlines or repeated phrases.
- **Do not distort your message to chase it.** Padding the pool with filler headlines to hit the highest rating can dilute the angles that win customers.
- **Judge by conversions and cost per conversion**, based on the actions you tracked, not by the label. If your tracking is not set up, fix that first; see our guide to [GA4 key events for forms, calls and WhatsApp enquiries](/blog/web-development-company-pune-ga4-key-events-form-call-whatsapp-lead-tracking-2026).

## Reading asset reports without fooling yourself

Google Ads provides asset-level reporting for RSAs, which labels assets such as headlines with performance ratings once enough data is available. Some sensible habits:

1. **Wait for data.** On a small account, a headline with a handful of impressions tells you nothing. Avoid pruning assets in the first couple of weeks or before they have had a meaningful number of impressions.
2. **Beware of the "Low" label.** A "Low" rating means the asset performed worse than others in the pool on the measured outcome, not that it is bad in absolute terms. It could also be an asset that is shown in the hardest searches.
3. **Look at conversions, not only clicks.** A headline that attracts curious clicks but few leads may be hurting you.
4. **Replace one or two assets at a time** so you can connect a change with a result. Rewriting the whole ad resets learning and makes cause and effect unreadable.
5. **Record changes with dates** in a simple sheet: what you changed, why, and what you expected.

Google's reporting methods change over time, so rely on the current Help documentation rather than any guide's description of exact labels.

## A testing routine for a small budget

Many Pune local businesses spend modest amounts, so each ad group may see only a modest number of clicks a month. Statistical certainty is out of reach for most. A pragmatic routine:

- **Month 1: build and observe.** Launch one RSA per ad group with a well-planned headline pool. Do not touch it for two to four weeks unless something is clearly wrong, such as disapprovals, wrong location targeting or irrelevant search terms.
- **Weeks 3 to 6: prune and add.** Use the search terms report to add negative keywords and adjust copy; replace the one or two weakest assets and add one new angle.
- **Monthly: review leads, not clicks.** Count qualified enquiries from calls, forms and WhatsApp, and compare to spend. Track the quality of leads, not only volume, with sales feedback if you can; see our note on [lead quality and offline conversions](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-quality-offline-conversions-2026).
- **Quarterly: refresh seasonal angles.** Festival, exam and monsoon periods change what people want. A Pune AC servicing ad in April is not the same message as in October.

If you must compare two ad versions properly, use Google Ads' experiment tools where available, change one meaningful thing, and keep the test running long enough to see a stable pattern. With small volumes, accept that some tests will be inconclusive, and do not declare a winner too early. For the landing-page side of testing with limited traffic, see [A/B testing with low traffic](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-landing-page-ab-testing-low-traffic-2026).

## A worked example with illustrative arithmetic

The numbers below are invented to show the reasoning. They are not benchmarks and not from any client.

Suppose a physiotherapy clinic in Pune spends ₹30,000 a month on Search ads for "back pain physiotherapy" in two nearby suburbs. In month one, the account records 600 clicks and 18 enquiries (calls, form fills and WhatsApp taps), and the clinic books 9 of them as appointments.

- Cost per click is ₹50 (30,000 divided by 600).
- Cost per enquiry is about ₹1,667 (30,000 divided by 18).
- Cost per booked appointment is about ₹3,333 (30,000 divided by 9).

Now suppose the search terms report shows a share of clicks coming from "physiotherapy jobs" and "physiotherapy course", and the asset report shows that headlines about "free assessment" have more conversions than headlines about "advanced equipment". The sensible response is not to rewrite everything; it is to add negative keywords for jobs and courses, add two more "assessment" and "first visit" headlines, and replace the weakest equipment headline. Next month, compare the cost per booked appointment, not the Ad Strength rating.

What matters is that the owner sees which number answers the business question: how much does it cost to fill an appointment slot? Clicks and impressions are only steps along the way.

## Common mistakes

- **Writing 15 versions of the same headline.** No variety, no learning.
- **Over-pinning.** Turning an RSA into a rigid ad and losing the system's flexibility.
- **Keyword insertion without checking the result.** Dynamic keyword insertion can produce awkward or inaccurate headlines and policy problems if the search term is not suitable; if you use it, review how it reads for your real search terms.
- **Promises the landing page does not keep.** "Free quote" with no quote form.
- **No negative keywords.** Money spent on job seekers and students.
- **Ignoring mobile.** Many local searches happen on phones; keep headlines short and make sure the page and the call button work on a phone.
- **Changing everything every week.** You cannot learn from noise.
- **Chasing Ad Strength** instead of leads.
- **Using a different brand voice in ads and on the site.** Visitors notice.
- **Claims in the ad that need proof you do not have**, such as rankings, awards or percentage results.

## Where RSAs fit with other campaign types

RSAs run in Search campaigns, where the searcher's words show intent. Other Google campaign types, such as Performance Max, assemble text and creative differently and rely more on automation; our overview of [Performance Max](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-performance-max-2026) explains where it fits and where a Search campaign with careful ad copy is still the safer first step for a small local budget. If you are just starting, a tightly themed Search campaign with well-written RSAs, correct conversion tracking and a landing page that matches is usually the clearest way to learn what works.

## Questions to ask your digital marketing agency in Pune

If you use a digital marketing agency in Pune or an independent specialist, a few questions separate careful management from routine:

- Can I see the headlines, descriptions and assets for each ad group, and which ones are pinned and why?
- How do you decide when to replace an asset?
- Which conversions are tracked, and do they include calls and WhatsApp taps?
- Do you share the search terms report and the negative keywords you have added?
- Is the account in my name, with me as the owner?
- What will you report each month, and does it include cost per qualified lead?

An agency that answers specifically and shares the data is easier to trust than one that offers only screenshots of impressions.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many headlines should a responsive search ad have?
Google allows up to 15 headlines and 4 descriptions. You do not have to use all 15, but provide enough distinct headlines to cover different angles: service, location, offer, proof and action. Fifteen near-duplicates add little.

### Should I pin headlines in a responsive search ad?
Only when you have a clear reason, such as a required legal statement or a brand-name rule. Pinning reduces the combinations Google can test. If you must pin, pin several alternatives to the same position rather than a single headline.

### Does Ad Strength affect how well my ads perform?
Ad Strength is Google's guide to the variety and relevance of your assets, not a guarantee of results. Use it to spot gaps, but judge performance by conversions and cost per conversion in your own account.

### How long should I wait before judging a responsive search ad?
Give an ad group several weeks and enough impressions and clicks to see a pattern, and avoid judging individual assets on a handful of impressions. On small budgets, expect slower learning and keep a dated record of changes.

### Can I use the same ad for different ad groups?
It is better to write the headlines and descriptions for each ad group's theme. A generic ad across unrelated keywords reduces relevance and click-through rate, which can raise costs.
